canberra.title: House of the Dragon’s third season finally lives up to the quality of early Game of Thrones
canberra.snippet: It has taken three seasons, but the Game of Thrones prequel House of the Dragon has finally provided a full season of quality akin to the...
canberra.content:
After two seasons of teasing, House of the Dragon’s third outing finally delivers on the epic scale of its source material. Photo: HBO Max.

It has taken three seasons, but the Game of Thrones prequel House of the Dragon has finally provided a full season of quality akin to the early seasons of its predecessor.

In its first two seasons, House of the Dragon (HotD) struggled to create its own identity. It couldn’t make up its mind whether it was purely an adaptation of George R.R. Martin’s fantasy encyclopedia, Fire and Blood, or its own separate thing, using key events as inspiration.

The show was stuck in limbo: despite some high-quality episodes and top-notch production, book fans were left frustrated by significant narrative changes, and casual fans were left unsure of just how dense and sophisticated the story was.

Honestly, with names like Aegon I, Aegon II, Aemond, Ormund, Rhaenys, Rhaenyra, Rhaena, Laena, and Helaena, it’s easy to see why.

Thankfully, with the show’s third season, the showrunners have learnt some valuable lessons, and in return, viewers were treated to a very good season of high-budget fantasy TV.

Throughout season three, we are given epic battles unlike anything ever seen on TV before. These character moments blur the lines between who is the real hero and who is the villain and, of course, include satisfying and shocking deaths for some of the most beloved and hated characters.

In previous seasons, particularly season 2, HotD was unable to manage the weight of so many characters and plots and, given the nature of the book it was based on, there was not much source material to draw from.

So many character decisions felt idiotic. The big moments were too few and far between, and there were too few things for each of the characters to do.

Thankfully, season three rectifies this by doing something really simple: focusing only on the main players and giving us a reason to care about them.

The main character of this entire show, Rhaenyra (Emma D’Arcy), finally becomes the primary focus. We are no longer jumping to 50 different characters just to fill a runtime. Instead, much of the season is told from her POV, giving the show proper direction.

It’s a small but important change of pace. For the first time in the show, the audience is given insight into how she feels, why she makes her decisions, and why she loses the plot.

D’Arcy gives an Emmy-worthy performance this time around, and it’s purely because she is given writing she can work with.

While D’Arcy takes centre stage, iconic characters like Daemon (Matt Smith) and Aemond (Ewan Mitchell) take a back seat. This is a positive thing.

Both are very mysterious and interesting elements of the show, but in the past, the writers have continued to give them screen time despite having little to do.

It made these great characters a chore to watch. But by giving Rhaenyra the focus, we find that when we do visit others, their presence feels so much more important.

The spectacle of this season is also far superior to its predecessors.

Season 1 was very much set up for the civil war that was to come. Season 2, for some reason, was even more of the same despite a lot of the pieces already being in place. Season 3 finally pulls the trigger.

There are three huge battles scattered across the season. They are among the best in the Game of Thrones franchise and made each episode feel like appointment viewing every Monday night.

The big set pieces made it easier for the writers too. The structure of the season became one episode of setup, the battle and then the fallout. It is simple but effective and provided a back-to-basics approach for the show that went too far into trying to be sophisticated.

The show has never been awful, but it’s never been as good as the original Game of Thrones until now. With one season left before HotD wraps up, viewers can only hope it carries this momentum into its final season.

All three seasons of House of the Dragon are now streaming on HBO Max.

canberra.title: Body corp goes to ACAT to force occupants to remove balcony screen
canberra.snippet: The body corporate of a large apartment complex has lost its attempt to force two occupants to remove a screen from their balcony, which ...
canberra.content:
23 August 2026

Join the conversation

1

The left image shows the screen on the occupants’ balcony. ACAT says the other two photos (centre, right) are example of screens having a negative impact on the visual amenity of a building. Photos: ACAT.

The body corporate of a large apartment complex has lost its attempt to force two occupants to remove a screen from their balcony, which they had placed there to reduce heat.

The occupants placed metal IKEA shelving, backed with screens, inside the enclosed balcony of their apartment in the 17-storey Civic complex, then put pot plants and planter boxes on the shelves.

But they ended up being taken to the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal (ACAT) when their body corporate tried to force them to remove it.

In a recently-published decision, Member Mark Hanna said the body corp argued the shelving violated the owners corporation rules and hadn’t been approved by the executive committee.

The body corp also sought an order to say the occupants could not put screens on their balcony without prior approval and wanted the occupants to pay the $379 used to start the proceedings.

Mr Hanna said the corporate was worried that approving structures like the occupants’ would allow other owners to erect similar screens and lower the appearance and property value of the complex.

The colour of the occupants’ installation did not blend correctly, it detracted from the aesthetic and monetary value of the property and it was clearly visible from the street, the corporate said.

ACAT heard there a long history between the parties before this application.

“The history is best summarised that the [occupants] have been for some time seeking to place some sort of screening on their enclosed balcony within their apartment to diminish the effects of the sun, lower the temperature and create a better environment within their apartment which has been opposed by the executive committee,” Mr Hanna said.

He said photos showed the occupants’ metal shelving was “barely visible” from the street.

“It is not visually disharmonious and blends in well with the colour and design of the current façade,” he said.

The occupants also said the shelving had reduced the temperature on the balcony and the impact of wind.

“As a result, we are able to open doors and our need for air-conditioning and heating is reduced,” they said.

“We have potted plants on the shelving including herbs and small vegetables. The small garden area greatly improves our quality of living.

“The shelving and screens allow us to more fully utilise all of the space available in our apartment.”

Mr Hanna ultimately denied the body corporate’s application to remove the shelving.

“[The] installation is freestanding, portable and not anchored to either a wall or floor. In this tribunal’s view the changes the installation makes to the apartment are cosmetic,” he said.

“If the executive committee were to order, as it urged the tribunal to do, to remove the items installed by the [occupants], it would be effectively behaving to unreasonably affect an owner’s lawful use and enjoyment of their unit.”

canberra.title: ‘One less needle, one less fear’: New ultrasound machines transform blood-taking for Canberra’s sickest patients
canberra.snippet: For many patients, having blood taken or an intravenous (IV) line inserted is a routine part of hospital care. But for others – particula...
canberra.content:
Dr Luke Streitberg demonstrates how Canberra Hospital’s new ultrasound-guided cannulation system helps clinicians locate veins in real time before inserting a needle. Photo: Naziya Alvi.

For many patients, having blood taken or an intravenous (IV) line inserted is a routine part of hospital care.

But for others – particularly cancer patients, older people, the obese or those with difficult-to-find veins – it can mean multiple painful attempts before a needle finally reaches its target.

Canberra Hospital hopes four new point-of-care ultrasound machines will change that.

Costing $50,000 each, the voice-activated machines have been purchased specifically for the Junior Medical Officer (JMO) Program and allow doctors to see a patient’s veins in real time, helping them guide a needle accurately into place.

Rather than relying on touch alone, doctors can now view the vein, surrounding tissue and even the needle as it enters the body.

The technology is expected to improve care for patients who traditionally face the greatest challenges with blood collection and IV cannulation, including oncology patients, people who are obese or hypotensive, and others with fragile veins. It also reduces the need to call in senior clinicians after hours when junior doctors struggle with difficult insertions.

Director of Prevocational Education and Training Dr Luke Streitberg said the idea grew out of lessons learned during the COVID-19 pandemic, when staff shortages made it harder to find experienced clinicians to assist with difficult cannulations.

“We instituted a program in 2023 with a tiny little handheld ultrasound to assist our junior medical officers, and it made a massive difference for both the patients and the JMOs,” he said.

However, those machines were fragile and prone to breaking easily. The new ones are expected to be sturdy.

While doctors will usually attempt a standard insertion first, they can proceed to ultrasound after two or three unsuccessful attempts, or immediately if a patient has a history of difficult access.

Unlike emergency departments, where senior emergency physicians and advanced trainees are available around the clock, hospital wards are often staffed predominantly by junior doctors overnight.

Dr Streitberg said the machines give junior clinicians another option before they need to escalate to senior staff.

The hospital currently has four machines positioned across its wards so they can be shared between teams after hours.

One feature that particularly impressed clinicians is the machines’ voice activation.

Unlike older systems that required doctors to touch an iPad or screen during a sterile procedure, the new units allow clinicians to adjust settings using voice commands.

“What this allows us to do is control aspects of the machine through voice commands, so you don’t need to touch it during an invasive procedure,” Dr Streitberg said.

“It’s really useful from an infection-control perspective.”

With Canberra’s population ageing and an increasing number of patients aged over 85 requiring hospital care, clinicians expect demand for the technology to continue to grow.

While most younger, healthy patients are unlikely to ever need ultrasound-guided cannulation, Dr Streitberg believes the machines will make a noticeable difference for those who do.

“For the patients who are the sickest and the hardest to cannulate, this is a game changer,” he said.

canberra.title: Should I pave my (gardening) paradise and put up a parking lot?
canberra.snippet: Thank goodness no one expects ROI reports on my hours spent gardening. Any analyst worth their weight in soil would immediately recommend...
canberra.content:
Gardening is about the journey, not the destination … which is good because mine is going nowhere fast. Photo: Hayley Nicholls.

Thank goodness no one expects ROI reports on my hours spent gardening.

Any analyst worth their weight in soil would immediately recommend we pave over my entire veggie patch and turn it into something more functional, like a parking lot.

Worm farms, compost heaps and sophisticated irrigation systems have thus far yielded only the occasional strawberry, entirely too much parsley, an unruly mint invasion and the occasional temper tantrum.

Oh, and zucchinis for days. But that’s entry-level stuff. Those hardy buggers will flourish, unsupervised and unloved, from a disused pile of pavers.

The fact is that most of my horticultural success stories have grown from a lack of effort, whereas seedlings I’ve treated like my own children have bitterly disappointed me (hopefully not like my own children).

Little sprouts lovingly tucked into their handmade egg boxes and milk carton beds along my windowsill, grown under the warm glow of my love and hydrated by hand, have – time and time again – raised my hopes daily only to die senselessly the second my back is turned.

Whereas, amongst the wilderness of my cottage garden, chicken enclosure or compost pile, several self-seeding baddies continue to pop up unbidden with all the familiarity and reliability of a multi-generational family living next door.

Each summer, without warning, festive shoots of amaranth burst into bloom like fireworks, turning my backyard into a curious landscape from Dr Seuss.

Seemingly at random, I find myself tripping over a robust asparagus stalk which has taken hold in an unlikely place. Seriously, are those things concreted in? If we do convert the plot, they’d make excellent parking bollards.

And of course, mint continues to darken my doorstep ever since I “propagated” a single sprig into a distant garden bed over 10 years ago. Ah, the naivety of gardening youth.

My chooks even appear to be more accomplished green thumbs (claws?) than I. Their seasonal patch of sprawling pumpkin plants and what must by now qualify as “heirloom” tomatoes taunt me.

I threw table scraps to my feathered friends, and this is how they repay me – rubbing their farm-to-table prowess in my face!

Anyway, none of that matters, which is why I just wrote 400 bitter words about it.

What matters is the practice of gardening.

The toil, trouble, peace and quiet. The satisfaction of weeding. The joy of prowling the garden centre for inspiration (or at least a new gnome). The validation of turning over a patch of soil you’ve been painstakingly improving, to find it rich and teeming with life. The strategy and planning as you lay adorable traps for tiny pests.

For example, did you know you can protect seedlings from snails and slugs by encircling them in crushed eggshells? It’s true. These precious pests don’t want to hurt their slimy little feet.

If you’d rather not risk injuring an innocent mollusc, you can repurpose recycled materials, like old yoghurt tubs, to construct walls that are intimidating enough to deter the most determined defoliator.

I get a mischievous sense of joy from laying such traps, giggling to myself as I punch the air like Macaulay Culkin in Home Alone.

At other times of year, I may be found bumbling around in the dark with my head torch on, constructing a haphazard shelter from a fitted sheet and old fence posts to protect prematurely planted seedlings against a late-season frost.

That’s a wholesome feeling.

Of course, the seedlings eventually die later anyway, thanks to birds, bugs, underwatering, overwatering, performance anxiety – honestly, who knows. But at least they knew they were loved.

Ultimately – even if it never produces a single edible growth – the mental, physical and creative benefits I get from tending my pointless little garden are enough to keep the bulldozers at bay.

No right-minded spreadsheet would ever favour the returns I get from my garden, but it’s still one of my best investments.

canberra.title: Rocket science: How Canberra’s becoming the powerhouse of Indoor Cricket in Australia
canberra.snippet: The ACT Rockets’ fourth consecutive Open Men’s Indoor Cricket title isn’t just a trophy – it highlights Canberra’s expanding ...
canberra.content:
23 August 2026

Start the conversation

That’s four! The victorious ACT Rockets. Photo: Supplied.

The ACT Rockets’ fourth consecutive Open Men’s Indoor Cricket title isn’t just a trophy – it highlights Canberra’s expanding dominance on the national stage.

The Rockets defeated Queensland 112 to 30 in the final, and the Rockets’ Brock Winkler won the player of the Grand Final for the third time.

The team’s record is incredible.

The ACT men’s side has lost just four games in four years, and the team has won seven National Open titles since 2015.

While notable, that athletic record is secondary to a far more profound influence beyond the arena.

Rocket’s head coach Billy Floros is also the Australian women’s head coach.

His assistant coach with the Rockets, Brenton Brian, is also the head coach of the Australian men’s team.

Rocket’s player, Vinesh Bennett, is the Australian men’s assistant coach with Kristen Bennett, the Australian women’s team trainer.

The ACT’s under 22 coach, Alexander Floros, is also the Australian women’s assistant coach.

Brock Winkler of the ACT Rockets. Photo: Supplied.

The Under 22 ACT Women's side pre-game. Photo: Supplied.

Nathan Kerr batting for the Rockets. Photo: Supplied.

Six ACT players have been named in the Australian men’s train-on squad ahead of next year’s trans-Tasman series in New Zealand, with several ACT players unavailable because of work and family commitments.

The ACT’s role in Australian indoor cricket has taken on an even greater dimension following the split from Cricket Australia.

Indoor cricket in Australia now comes under the auspices of Australian Indoor Cricket.

The newly formed national organisation has Canberra’s Cameron Walter as the chair, with Billy Floros a board director.

Canberra has also been awarded the hosting rights for the 2027 Men’s and Women’s Opens and the Men’s and Women’s under 22 championships, with games to be played at Action Indoor Sports Kambah.

It’s the first time the Open level nationals have been staged in Canberra since 1991, further enhancing the ACT’s emerging presence in the sport previously the domain of Queensland, Victoria, Western Australia and NSW.

Success at the men’s open level, though, shouldn’t mask an obvious shortcoming in the sport in Canberra, with no ACT Women’s Open team competing at the nationals since 1996.

The hope is that the under-22 women’s side, which competed at the nationals this year, will ensure the ACT has an Open Women’s team for next year’s championships in Canberra.

australia.title: Swans fans turn up to support women’s team – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Victorian Labor expands on free dental care election promise The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll , and health mini...
australia.content:
Swans fans turn out to support women’s team

Jack Larkin

Sydney Swans fans have gathered at the SCG for a historic double-header as a cloud hangs over the club amid a scandal that has shaken Australian football.

Five AFL players – Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon – have been stood down for the rest of the season by the Swans for breaching the club’s standards, including drinking and bringing women back to their hotel after their round 23 win over Essendon.

Sydney’s AFLW side is taking on Essendon on Sunday at the SCG before the men’s side closes out its regular season against North Melbourne.

As the teams prepare for the highly anticipated double header, lifelong fans have been wrestling with whether to show their support for the men’s side.

Daniel, a member for 26 years, said he would be staying for both games.

I will be watching both. It’s ultimately a club. It’s ultimately both teams. I think it’s the fact that those five players are not out there which made me comfortable to stay to watch the men’s game.

Shayal, another Swans member, said she felt a sombre mood on the light rail heading to the game:

I’m only planning to stay for the women’s game and then leaving before the men’s game. I’ve been a member for over 10 years, and it just doesn’t feel right. And I’m not sure if I’ll renew my membership again.

Some fans at the AFLW match held signs supporting women, including one that read: “The Swans are nothing without W.”

Key events

  • 3h ago

    What we learned, Sunday 23 August

  • 4h ago

    Swans fans turn out to support women’s team

  • 5h ago

    Sydney Marathon admits ‘unfortunate error’ on medal depicting Munich stadium

  • 6h ago

    Concern Sydney Marathon medal may erroneously depict Munich stadium

  • 7h ago

    Seal confirmed first mammal death from bird flu in Australia

  • 7h ago

    One Nation MP ‘impressed’ with PM after rice factory rescue promise

  • 7h ago

    First exhibitions on display at new Powerhouse Parramatta museum in Sydney

  • 8h ago

    Victorian Liberals announce plan for new appeals court to ensure tougher sentences

  • 8h ago

    Good morning

What we learned, Sunday 23 August

And that’s where we’ll leave you this afternoon. Here’s what we learned today:

  • A long-nosed fur seal has died from H5 bird flu in South Australia, marking the first confirmed case in a mammal on the Australian mainland.

  • Sydney Swans fans gathered at the SCG for a historic double-header as a cloud hangs over the club amid a scandal that has shaken Australian football.

  • The Victorian premier announced $12.9m to grow and retain the workforce required to operate the 10 free public dental clinics promised if it is re-elected in November.

  • The Victorian Liberals have said they will split the court of appeal in two if they win the election.

  • Sydney Marathon has admitted an “unfortunate error” that saw its participation medal depicting a stadium in Munich, instead of Sydney.

  • Powerhouse Parramatta has unveiled its inaugural exhibition program.

  • A 46-year-old Melton man driving a stolen car has died following a fatal collision in East Melbourne overnight.

Thanks so much for your company today. We’ll be back bright and early tomorrow morning. See you then.

Sarah Basford Canales

One Nation seeks to explain MP’s migration comments

One Nation has sought to explain its immigration policy after comments by Farrer MP, David Farley, caused some confusion this morning.

Farley told ABC’s Insiders One Nation’s net overseas migration (Nom) target was 130,000 but said an additional 100,000 migrant workers, including skilled workers and backpackers, were not included in that figure. The first-term One Nation MP said the final Nom was “not too different” to the Albanese government’s.

In a social media post on Sunday afternoon, the party stated the cuts would come from “fewer international students and dependants [sic], a dramatic reduction in temporary graduate visas and their dependants [sic], and a much more targeted skilled migration program focused on the skills Australia genuinely needs”.

The post continued:

Short-term seasonal agricultural workers who do not meet the ABS residency test are not counted in net overseas migration. They come for limited periods, often live on farms or regional properties while they work, and return home.

One Nation’s target is less than half Labor’s current level.

Labor opened the floodgates to mass migration and has repeatedly blown its own migration forecasts since coming to government.

The statement isn’t quite true. Short-term seasonal agricultural workers – for example, backpackers who might pick fruit as part of a working holiday – do count in the Nom figure if they stay within Australia for 12 months over a 16-month period.

Sydney Swans play first game since men’s team scandal

The Sydney Swans’ women’s and men’s teams are taking to the field at the SCG for a double-header as controversy swirls around the club.

We’ll have more reporting soon, but photos from the ground give a sense of the mood as the AFLW game got under way.

Zoe Daniel blasts major parties

Today we feature a scathing opinion piece by former independent MP Zoe Daniel.

Daniel argues that the events in Canberra over the last sitting week – which saw Labor and the Coalition coming together to push through legislation on gambling, on the NDIS and on the power of digital companies – are “evidence that the two-party system is cooked”.

“Government and opposition prioritise political survival over community concern,” Daniel says.

“They choose to swallow their hatred of each other to safeguard their collective mediocrity.”

Sydney Marathon admits ‘unfortunate error’ on medal depicting Munich stadium

Organisers of next weekend’s Sydney Marathon have said they are “not going to run from” the “unfortunate error” that saw a stadium in Germany represented on their participation medal, instead of the very similarly named stadium in Sydney.

As we reported earlier, one side of the recently revealed medal appears to feature a stadium that looks like the Allianz Arena in Munich, Germany, rather than Allianz Stadium in Sydney (which the marathon route passes).

A TCS Sydney Marathon spokesperson said in a statement just now that they “can’t wait” for the event on 30 August, and:

You may also be aware that a little too much international flavour has found its way onto the back of the finishers medal, with an incorrect depiction of the stadium. We’re not going to run from it, it was an unfortunate error, though it’s certainly given everyone something to talk about this weekend, mostly in good humour.

With the event a week away, this is the medal our finishers will receive. It’s a beautiful medal, and now a little more unique. What it represents does not change. Behind every one of these medals is months of early mornings, long runs and quiet determination, and having it placed around your neck at the Sydney Opera House is a moment our participants will never forget. Whether it’s a first marathon or a seventh Major, every person who crosses that line has earned something no detail in the artwork could ever take away.

We’re grateful to our participants and partners for taking it in such good humour, and our focus now is where it should be, on delivering a safe, spectacular and unforgettable weekend for the 40,000 people lining up on Sunday and the hundreds of thousands of spectators along our course. As Australia’s largest marathon, this is shaping up to be our biggest and best year yet, and we can’t wait to welcome the world to Sydney.

Benita Kolovos

Ben Carroll rejects Victorian Liberals’ proposal to split court of appeal as ‘thought bubble’

Victoria’s premier Ben Carroll was asked this morning about the Liberal party’s proposal to split the court of appeal in two and appoint new judges if they win the election.

He says the Labor government has already reformed bail laws and is reviewing sentencing, leaving the Liberals “floundering”. Carroll went on:

The Liberal party are upset that we’ve captured the law and order agenda. And now they’re saying we’re going to skip that process and go to the court of appeal. That’s why they’ve had this thought bubble overnight, and they will not be able to explain it. That’s the simple truth … Let’s wait and see what all the legal stakeholders say about Mr Newbury’s new policy.

Carroll, who is trained as a lawyer, questioned how the Liberal party would reform a court that “has been around [for] 200 years, and rewrite case law overnight”. He said:

It shows you the Liberal party today have no legal expertise, but [are] totally at sea on having a policy agenda for the next election, and are floundering. We’ve seen today the Liberal party searching for a policy idea and not doing any homework.

Sarah Basford Canales

Fur seal death ‘not unexpected’ as H5 bird flu spreads, federal agriculture minister says

The federal agriculture minister, Julie Collins, says the death of a fur seal in South Australia from H5 bird flu is “not unexpected” as the virus begins to spread through wild seabirds.

Speaking a short time ago in Hobart, Collins said the “distressing” news of the first confirmed case of a mammal on the mainland was anticipated and that it is “not possible to avoid significant losses”.

She said:

An infection of this individual animal is likely to have occurred due to exposure to infected wild birds or the environment that they share ... as I’ve been clear, we can’t stop it spreading in terms of, particularly, in wild birds, and where we see more dead wild birds, we do expect to see increased reports of marine mammals.

Collins said there had been 298 events across the country with 183 in South Australia, 86 in Victoria, 11 in New South Wales, 10 in Western Australia, seven in Tasmania and one in Queensland.

The risk to human health remains low.

Benita Kolovos

Victorian Labor expands on free dental care election promise

The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, and health minister, Ingrid Stitt, have held a press conference this morning off the back of their announcement yesterday that the Labor government would open 10 free public dental clinics if re-elected in November.

Today, they’ve announced $12.9m to grow and retain the workforce required to operate the 10 clinics. The government estimates it will need 180 full-time equivalent workers to keep the 10 clinics running from 9am to 9pm on weekdays and 9am to 5pm on weekends.

Stitt said the funds would include $2.1m for relocation support for 20 dental clinicians for the three regional clinics, $3.8m to fund 30 dental assistant traineeships and 20 dental graduate placements for the next two years and $4.4m to attract and retain existing staff.

Carroll said that while some Victorians can access public dental care, the group was limited, adding:

You can’t use a Medicare card for dental unless you’ve got a healthcare card or you are a category of a particular citizen, it is very difficult … I’ve been visiting a lot of dentists over the past few weeks. There [are] waiting lists. People are in enormous, unbearable pain.

This will be a cost of living measure but it will also make sure that we deal with the healthcare of some of the most vulnerable Victorians. This is really going to fill the gap that’s been there for decades.

Concern Sydney Marathon medal may erroneously depict Munich stadium

Just a week away from the Sydney Marathon, speculation has been growing that a stadium in Munich may have been erroneously etched on to the event’s participation medal instead of a local Sydney landmark.

In an Instagram post on the official Sydney Marathon account earlier this week, revealing the design of the participation medal, runners were told they would “find the story of the course in the details” of the design:

The markings around the edge represent each kilometre of the course, while the eight circles on the back represent the Abbott World Marathon Majors. A beautiful Sydney skyline brings the course to life, featuring the landmarks runners will experience along the way – starting with the Sydney Harbour Bridge and finishing at the world-famous Sydney Opera House.

But as the BBC reported on Saturday, the “landmarks” side of the medal appears to feature a stadium that looks like the Allianz Arena in Munich, Germany, rather than Allianz Stadium in Sydney (which the marathon route passes).

The reverse of the medal features an indigo and gold design by First Nations artist Ambrose Killian, representing kilometres of the course, and the eight global major marathons. Killian told the BBC he was not involved in the other side of the design.

The marathon will take place on 30 August. In 2025, about 35,000 marathoners from more than 120 countries participated in the event – the first year as a World Marathon major event.

Guardian Australia has approached Sydney Marathon for comment.

Andrew Messenger

A new scheme is about to replace the NDIS for children with autism. Why has Queensland refused to sign up?

As parliament debated the future of the National Disability Insurance Scheme this week, Ali Kuylaars was worried.

Her two children, both diagnosed with autism, could be among thousands across the country removed from the federal scheme by January 2028.

But Isaac, 14, and Arlo, eight, live in Queensland, the last holdout state not to sign up for a new replacement scheme, known as Thriving Kids.

Intended to assist children with mild to moderate autism or developmental delays up to the age of nine, Thriving Kids is scheduled to be implemented from October this year, fully replacing the NDIS for those children by 2028.

But the Queensland premier, David Crisafulli, still has questions about the new program, and says he won’t sign up without answers. Some are concerned that the dispute won’t be resolved quickly enough, leaving Queensland children to fall into a gap between ineligibility for the NDIS and a delayed implementation of Thriving Kids.

But others are concerned about the new scheme itself, and argue the state government is taking the right approach by demanding more information.

Read the full story here:

Seal confirmed first mammal death from bird flu in Australia

Lisa Cox

A long-nosed fur seal has died from H5 bird flu in South Australia, marking the first confirmed case in a mammal on the Australian mainland.

The fur seal was found dead at Beachport on Wednesday on the state’s Limestone Coast.

It marks a fresh escalation in the spread of the virus days after the South Australian premier, Peter Malinauskas, announced three mass mortality events on offshore islands involving more than 1,000 greater crested terns.

The highly pathogenic strain of bird flu has killed millions of birds globally and crossed over into mammal species, including elephant seals.

Long-nosed fur seals and the endangered Australian sea lion are among the mammal species the federal government has assessed as facing very high risk from the virus.

The SA government has also confirmed a little penguin found at Kangaroo Island this week tested positive for H5 bird flu.

One Nation MP ‘impressed’ with PM after rice factory rescue promise

Sarah Basford Canales

David Farley says he was “impressed” with Anthony Albanese after receiving an in-person guarantee from the prime minister that the Labor government would help out rice factories in his electorate.

Rice producer SunRice announced 78 workers would be sacked from mills in Leeton and Deniliquin this week, but ABC’s Insiders host, David Speers, says a funding package is being prepared to help out the producer and save those jobs.

Farley said:

I was impressed how Albanese at the Governor-General’s event the other night came straight up to me and said, ‘Look, I’m aware of it. I’m working on it. We’ll get it done’ ... even after, as we left the chamber the other day, we spoke all the way across to the Senate talking about it. How could it be done and put together? So you know, I tilt my hat to them.

Sarah Basford Canales

David Farley rejects claim One Nation has no serious policies

The One Nation MP David Farley has rejected claims from Liberal Andrew Hastie that his party has no serious policies and only “thought bubbles”.

Appearing on ABC’s Insiders this morning, the member for Farrer said:

Those policies are there … There’s a powerful amount of work goes on it.

Farley also suggested the minor party’s net migration target is closer to 230,000 in order to include backpackers, Pacific workers, and more skilled workers.

He said One Nation’s net overseas migration (Nom) target is 130,000, plus a minimum of about 100,000 workers.

He continued:

We’re focusing on the Nom in its true form, and then we’ve got these programs that have been available now for over a decade that drive our economy … the raw number is not too different, but the reality is, where do we need them? We don’t need them in the great urban metroplex. We need them out to be productive, working in agriculture, engineering, mining, etc.

Before being elected, Farley said Australia’s net overseas migration of 306,000 last year was “probably not” too many. The party’s leader, Pauline Hanson, said she had a conversation with him about the comments.

Man driving stolen car in Melbourne dies in crash

A 46-year-old Melton man driving a stolen car has died following a fatal collision in East Melbourne overnight, according to Victoria police.

The man was seen in the Richmond area of Melbourne on Saturday night “erratically” driving a stolen white Subaru, which was bearing false plates and had been stolen from Glen Iris on 20 August, police said in a statement early this morning.

The man, reportedly travelling on the wrong side of the road at the time, then collided with two vehicles, one of which was a Mustang, near Punt Road and Boulton Parade at about 9pm.

He got out of the crashed vehicle and jumped into the Mustang before driving off, police said. The driver of the Mustang wasn’t injured or in the vehicle at the time.

The man continued driving erratically in the stolen Mustang on to Barassi Way where he collided head on with a Range Rover and then into a Toyota Camry. He was ejected from the Mustang and died at the scene, police said.

The driver of the Range Rover received an injury to her arm and was taken to hospital. The other motorist was not injured.

Police are also following up reports the vehicle was seen driving erratically in Clarendon and Whiteman streets prior to the first collision, and have appealed for any witnesses to the collision or with dashcam footage to contact Crime Stoppers.

First exhibitions on display at new Powerhouse Parramatta museum in Sydney

Powerhouse Parramatta – a museum and gallery project 12 years and $915m in the making – has unveiled its inaugural exhibition program. The five exhibitions focus on “immersive” experiences, including 3D cityscape, a crystal tunnel and historic aeroplanes.

Powerhouse describes the forthcoming exhibitions as follows:

  • The Dark: an immersive exhibition created for children aged 4 – 12 years old. Developed in collaboration with creatives Kip Williams, Elizabeth Gadsby and Marg Horwell, The Dark is a bedroom, a crystal tunnel, a forest, and a gateway to a land of giants. It is magical with many things to be discovered one by one.

  • Es Devlin: The Turning is an exhibition of 5 major works by British artist, Es Devlin whose genre-defying work ranges from sculpture to film, architecture, language and performance. Her work immerses audiences into atmospheric environments that draw on Earth’s vast biodiversity, maths and our collective imaginations.

  • Overflow: A First Nations-led exhibition grounded in the living principles of Water Country, working with seven Aboriginal organisations to consider the importance and care of salt and freshwater systems throughout NSW. These stories are brought to life through the cinematic lens of acclaimed film-maker and Kamilaroi man Ivan Sen.

  • Task Eternal: will explore the intersection of design, innovation and technology and trace humanity’s quest to defy gravity, take flight and journey into the sky.

  • The Mall: across two storeys, the exhibition examines the history, evolution and cultural significance of the shopping mall, exploring Australian and global innovation across architecture, design, technology, engineering, and fashion.

The institution isn’t scheduled to open its doors until 7 November. Admission will be free, but visitors aged 16 or over will be charged a fee to see Task Eternal.

Lisa Havilah, Powerhouse’s chief executive said in a statement this morning:

Powerhouse Parramatta will redefine how museums connect with community, industry and learning. As Western Sydney’s first NSW cultural institution, it will be a place that celebrates the creativity, ambition and diversity of our communities, connecting local stories and knowledge with international innovation.

These five foundational exhibitions place audiences at the heart of the museum, bringing to life stories of technology, creativity and excellence. Together, they reflect our ambition to create a museum that amplifies community, creates new opportunities and helps define the future. We are deeply grateful to our patrons for their visionary support and for joining us on the journey to create one of the world’s great new museums. We can’t wait to open the doors this November.

Victorian Liberals announce plan for new appeals court to ensure tougher sentences

Benita Kolovos

The Victorian Liberals have announced they will split the court of appeal in two and appoint new judges if they win the election, saying a separate one for criminal matters would match “community expectations”.

The opposition leader, Jess Wilson, will today announce a plan for two separate appeal courts – criminal and civil – and appoint additional judges specialising in criminal matters to the former.

The Coalition said the new court of criminal appeal would have “broad oversight across Victoria’s courts” to ensure “sentences for serious crime match community expectations” and give effect to new bail and sentencing laws they would enact before Christmas.

They argue the decisions of this court would then flow down through the entire system, pushing up sentences handed out in courts across the state.

Wilson said:

Our new criminal court will empower specialist criminal law judges to ensure sentencing of criminals meet community expectations. Each sentence they hand down will form part of case law going forward, helping to establish appropriate consequences for criminal actions.

Good morning

Welcome to Guardian Australia’s Sunday live news blog. My name is Stephanie Convery, and I’ll be with you until this afternoon.

A man driving a stolen vehicle has died after a fatal collision in East Melbourne overnight, Victoria police said this morning. The man was seen driving a stolen white Subaru “erratically” in the Richmond area before he collided with two vehicles near Punt Road and Boulton Parade about 9pm, police said.

The Sydney Swans – both the men’s and the women’s teams – will be back on the field today in a double header intended to celebrate the success of the AFLW team, but which has been overshadowed this week by the off-field behaviour of some members of the men’s team.

And the new Powerhouse Parramatta museum in Sydney has unveiled its inaugural exhibition program ahead of its official opening in November.

Grab a coffee, and we’ll bring you more on all of those shortly.

australia.title: Liberal plan to split Victorian appeals court attacked as ‘thought bubble’ that would politicise judiciary
australia.snippet: Opposition leader Jess Wilson says new dedicated court of criminal appeal would set precedents for tougher sentences Get our breaking new...
australia.content:
A radical overhaul of Victoria’s highest court, proposed by the Liberal party to increase sentences, has been criticised by legal and human rights groups who warn it would politicise the judiciary.

The opposition leader, Jess Wilson, on Sunday announced that if elected in November the Coalition would split the court of appeal in two, creating a dedicated court of criminal appeal alongside a separate court of civil appeal.

It would appoint additional judges with expertise in criminal law to the new court of criminal appeal.

The overhaul would be introduced alongside tougher bail and sentencing laws, which the Coalition has committed to enacting before the end of the year if it wins government.

Together, the measures would help set new legal precedents which the Coalition said would ultimately lead to tougher sentences for serious offences.

“It’s time for a new approach,” Wilson said on Sunday. “Our new criminal court will empower specialist criminal law judges to ensure sentencing of criminals meet community expectations. Each sentence they hand down will form part of case law going forward, helping to establish appropriate consequences for criminal actions.

In Victoria, judges are appointed by the governor on the recommendation of the attorney general. The shadow attorney general, James Newbury, said “nothing will change” about that process, though a “strong background in criminal matters will be a key focus” when making appointments.

“[It] will mean that criminal matters are dealt with by specialist judges who will be tough on crime, who will be tough on criminal offences,” he said.

Newbury said he had “consulted in a way that Victorians would expect” with judges and the courts about the policy, though he said it would be inappropriate to discuss the consultation publicly.

Legal and human rights groups, however, have criticised the proposal.

Gemma Cafarella, the president of Liberty Victoria, described it as a “dangerous and ignorant thought bubble designed without the input of experts”.

She said in “properly functioning democracies” parliaments make the laws and courts apply them, with the two systems kept seperate.

“Governments shouldn’t choose judges to get the outcomes they want,” Cafarella said. “This is a move that would politicise the criminal courts, and it must be rejected.”

She said the comments by the Coalition were by implication an “appalling political attack on the work of court of appeal judges”.

The Australian Lawyers Alliance criminal justice spokesperson, Greg Barns SC, said there was “no clear evidence” the court of appeal structure was failing, “aside from the longstanding issue of underfunding”.

“This is a disturbing example of the risk of undermining the independence of the judiciary,” he said. “It sends a signal that the opposition is willing to interfere with judicial independence for political purposes.”

The Alliance’s director, Susan Accary, said they were “not persuaded” splitting the courts would improve the quality of justice or address delays in the system.

Tom Ballantyne, president of the Law Institute of Victoria, said it was unclear how the proposal “adds anything” to the court of appeal, as it “already has access to numerous judges with extensive criminal expertise”.

“Anything that could undermine the independence of the courts and its judges could have significant consequences and would be a significant concern to the community,” he said.

Earlier this month One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, said the party wanted to make “bleeding heart judges accountable” and “get rid” of those he believes fail to meet community expectations.

Crime continues to be a major issue in the lead-up to the November election, with the Labor government having already passed controversial “adult time for violent crime” and tougher bail laws. It is also undertaking a review of sentencing.

The premier, Ben Carroll, on Sunday said the new policy showed the Liberal party was “floundering”.

He questioned how the opposition could “rewrite case law overnight”.

“It shows you the Liberal party today have no legal expertise,” Carroll said.

australia.title: Hanson forced to intervene after One Nation MP says party’s migration target ‘not too different’ from Labor’s
australia.snippet: David Farley says party wants 100,000 migrant rural workers in addition to the 130,000 migration target it considers the ‘true’ number Fo...
australia.content:
The One Nation MP David Farley says the minor party’s net migration target is “not too different” to Labor’s, forcing his leader to issue an urgent clarification amid rising confusion over the policy.

It is the second time Pauline Hanson has had to issue a correction after the member for Farrer seemed to contradict One Nation’s restrictive approach to immigration.

Appearing on the ABC’s Insiders program on Sunday morning, Farley argued skilled workers and backpackers were critical to keeping Australia fed, and argued they should be considered as a separate category to migration “in its true form”.

The minor rightwing party, led by Hanson, has struggled to define its migration policy, with inconsistent messaging over whether its target figure represents net overseas migration (Nom) or permanent migration.

The member for Farrer said One Nation’s Nom target remained 130,000. But he said that figure did not include skilled workers, backpackers and Pacific and Timor-Leste labour through the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (Palm) scheme.

Farley said he expected there would be room for a “minimum” 100,000 additional people in the migration target to ensure critical industries had enough workers. Those included about 40,000 Palm workers and 70,000 skilled workers, including aged care nurses.

“A minimum of 100 [thousand additional migrant workers], but the 130,000 [target] is what we call the true Nom,” he told ABC’s Insiders on Sunday.

“I think the big difference is [that] we’re focusing on: what are the skills we need as a nation, where do we need these migrants to be.

“The raw number is not too different [to the government’s], but the reality is, where do we need them? We don’t need them in the great urban metroplex. We need them out to be productive, working in agriculture, engineering, mining.”

But Hanson issued an implied rebuke to her MP on Sunday afternoon, with a post on social media insisting “One Nation’s policy is to cut net overseas migration to 130,000”.

Hanson said: “Short-term seasonal agricultural workers who do not meet the ABS residency test are not counted in net overseas migration.”

In fact, seasonal workers who live in Australia for 12 months over a 16-month period are included in the Nom.

The Nom is calculated by the difference between the number of people entering and leaving the country who have lived in or out of the country for 12 months over a 16-month period. It includes Australians moving abroad and returning but excludes short-term visitors, such as tourists.

The Nom is different to permanent migration, which measures longer-term visas offered to skilled workers and family members. For this financial year, there are 185,000 permanent places.

The shadow home affairs minister, Jonno Duniam, said One Nation has “somehow managed to turn one headline number (130,000) into at least half a dozen different immigration policies”.

“One Nation is having extraordinary difficulty answering the most basic question of all: how many migrants would actually come to Australia under its policy?” he said.

Energy minister, Chris Bowen, said: “I’m not sure what One Nation is saying about immigration because it appears to me, based on what Mr Farley said, that One Nation now agrees with the approach of the government. And obviously I’d welcome that.”

The Nom figure surged after the pandemic, during which it fell below zero, but has began to return to more typical levels in recent quarters.

The Nom was forecast to drop to 295,000 people last financial year but reached 301,000. The government forecasts it to drop further to 245,000 in 2026-27 and 225,000 in 2027-28.

The Albanese government is preparing to announce changes to the migration system to achieve Nom targets.

The Coalition has declined to provide an exact figure for its Nom target, but the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, has indicated it will be “well below 200,000”.

One Nation’s immigration policy is listed as offering a hard visa cap of 130,000 a year – a policy that would probably lead to a negative Nom. Barnaby Joyce, a former Nationals MP who defected to One Nation last December, has suggested the 130,000 number was instead a target for the Nom.

Farley’s electorate in south-western NSW relies on migrant workers for aged care and food processing. The Farrer MP said more than two-thirds of workers in his seat’s slaughterhouses and processing units were migrants.

“We need to have dexterity and flexibility in it. Managed properly, [the migration system] works well … we’re talking a system that’s critical to Australia. It’s critical to our food,” he said.

Before being elected, Farley said Australia’s net overseas migration of 306,000 last year was “probably not” too many.

Hanson later said she had counselled him on the comments, while Joyce described them as a slip-up during the “pressure of a campaign”.

On Sunday, Farley also said he was “impressed” by Anthony Albanese after the prime minister reassured him in person of a planned bailout for rice mills in his electorate.

Farley was also asked about Hanson’s decision to appeal to the high court against a finding that she racially discriminated against Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi, and whether discrimination laws should allow people to offend, insult or humiliate someone based on race.

He said: “Well, I’m not convinced that we need to go and change anything at the moment.”

australia.title: Sydney Marathon admits ‘unfortunate error’ as finisher’s medal depicts Munich stadium as race highlight
australia.snippet: ‘Landmarks’ side of the medal features the Allianz Arena in German city rather than Allianz Stadium in Sydney Follow our Australia news l...
australia.content:
In a week’s time, the proud runners finishing the Sydney Marathon will receive a medal showing the landmarks they have just sped past – plus one they definitely didn’t.

In what organisers have admitted was an “unfortunate error”, a stadium in Munich, Germany, was erroneously etched on to the event’s participation medal instead of a local Sydney landmark.

In an Instagram post on the official Sydney Marathon account earlier this week, revealing the design of the participation medal, runners were told they would “find the story of the course in the details” of the design.

“A beautiful Sydney skyline brings the course to life, featuring the landmarks runners will experience along the way,” the post reads, “starting with the Sydney Harbour Bridge and finishing at the world-famous Sydney Opera House”.

However, one of the “landmarks” on the medal is the Allianz Arena in Munich, Germany, rather than Allianz Stadium in Sydney (which the marathon route passes).

“A little too much international flavour has found its way onto the back of the finisher’s medal, with an incorrect depiction of the stadium,” a TCS Sydney Marathon spokesperson said on Sunday.

“We’re not going to run from it, it was an unfortunate error, though it’s certainly given everyone something to talk about this weekend, mostly in good humour.”

The error was reported by the BBC and noted with amusement by several running blogs. The Munich stadium, which opened in 2005 and is home to the Bayern Munich football team, responded in the comments of one: “Oh wow, we didn’t have that on our bingo card!”

The reverse of the medal features an indigo and gold design by First Nations artist Ambrose Killian, representing kilometres of the course, and the eight global major marathons. Killian told the BBC he was not involved in the other side of the design.

The marathon will take place on 30 August. In 2025, about 35,000 marathoners from more than 120 countries participated in the event – its first year as a World Marathon major event.

Sydney Marathon organisers said it was “a beautiful medal, and now a little more unique”.

“What it represents does not change,” the spokesperson said. “Behind every one of these medals is months of early mornings, long runs and quiet determination, and having it placed around your neck at the Sydney Opera House is a moment our participants will never forget.

“We’re grateful to our participants and partners for taking it in such good humour, and our focus now is where it should be, on delivering a safe, spectacular and unforgettable weekend [event].”

It’s not the first time official medals have run into problems. In 2012, some of the 23,000 runners in the Edinburgh marathon remarked on the rather phallic profile of their finisher’s award.

Earlier this year, the Winter Olympics were plagued by reports of cracking and snapping medals. And in Paris in 2024 the bronze medals were replaced after they quickly discoloured.

australia.title: Fur seal’s death marks first Australian mainland mammal fatality from spreading H5 bird flu strain
australia.snippet: Seal found dead at Beachport in South Australia presages ‘significant losses’, minister warns Follow our Australia news live blog for lat...
australia.content:
A long-nosed fur seal has died from H5 bird flu in South Australia, marking the first confirmed case in a mammal on the Australian mainland.

The seal was found dead at Beachport on Wednesday on the state’s Limestone Coast.

It marks a fresh escalation in the spread of the virus days after the South Australian premier, Peter Malinauskas, announced three mass mortality events on offshore islands involving more than 1,000 greater crested terns.

The federal agriculture minister, Julie Collins, said the seal death was “not unexpected” as the virus begins to spread through the country.

Speaking in Hobart on Sunday, Collins said the “distressing” news of the first confirmed case of a mammal on the mainland was anticipated and that it was “not possible to avoid significant losses”.

“An infection of this individual animal is likely to have occurred due to exposure to infected wild birds or the environment that they share,” she said.

“We can’t stop it spreading in terms of, particularly, in wild birds, and where we see more dead wild birds, we do expect to see increased reports of marine mammals.”

Collins said there had been 298 events across the country, with 183 in South Australia, 86 in Victoria, 11 in New South Wales, 10 in Western Australia, seven in Tasmania and one in Queensland.

The risk of human transmission remains low, but people are being urged to avoid sick or dead birds and report them to birdflu.gov.au.

The long-nosed fur seal was found dead with no signs of injury and reported to an official hotline by a member of the public on Wednesday

Testing of samples from the seal later confirmed the H5 bird flu detection.

The highly pathogenic strain of bird flu has killed millions of birds globally and crossed over into mammal species, including elephant seals.

Long-nosed fur seals and the endangered Australian sea lion are among the mammal species the federal government has assessed as facing very high risk from the virus.

Jack Gough, the chief executive of the Invasive Species Council, said the virus spreading to Australia’s sea lion population could be an “extinction level event”.

“We are still just at the early stages of this devastating virus, and the bad news is going to keep coming for our wildlife as it spreads around the continent and between species,” he said.

The SA government has also confirmed a little penguin found at Kangaroo Island this week tested positive for H5 bird flu.

The SA’s environment minister, Emily Bourke, said the state would work with the federal government to assess whether an experimental vaccine from the United States could be used for mammals in Australia.

“It is not an off-the-shelf vaccine that’s been approved, and we have to be taking into consideration the risk [of undertaking] the vaccination program in our mammals,” she said.

Australian Marine Conservation Society campaign director, Alexia Wellbelove, urged the federal government to create a $200m wildlife resilience fund for threatened species at risk of mass mortalities or local extinctions.

“Government preparedness funding got us this far, but it was never designed to manage active spread across multiple species and states,” Wellbelove said.

Elsewhere, the Tasmanian government said 51 little penguins found on the state’s King Island were “assumed to” have died from H5 bird flu, but the deaths would not be declared a mass mortality event.

The state’s natural resources and environment department said a sample taken from one penguin found at the Port of Grassy tested positive for H5 bird flu, while a sample from a second penguin was inconclusive.

Wes Ford, the state’s incident controller for its bird flu response, said both samples had been sent to the Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness for further testing.

“The little penguin mortality event is not considered a mass mortality event, and the condition of the remaining deceased birds meant they were unsuitable for testing,” he said.

“As a result, the cause of death could not be confirmed, although it may be assumed to have been from bird flu.

“Our teams continue to monitor reports of sick and dead birds closely, with results from surveillance informing our response.”

world.title: US deports 20 people to Liberia, the first of 1,200 migrants under Trump deal
world.snippet: Agreement is among largest third-country deportations driven by Trump administration’s immigration crackdown Twenty deportees from the Un...
world.content:
Twenty deportees from the United States arrived in Liberia on Thursday, as part of a new agreement that will see the west African country receive as many as 1,200 people under the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

The group arrived at the Roberts international airport outside the capital, Monrovia. The Liberia-US agreement is one of the largest third-country deportation arrangements pursued by the administration since Trump returned to office last year.

The Liberian information minister, Jerolinmek Piah said the 1,200 deportees will include African nationals as well as nationals from North America, South America and the Caribbean.

During a briefing on Tuesday, Liberia’s justice minister, Natu Oswald Tweh, said that the majority of the deportees had committed migration-related violations and offenses, and that they could seek asylum in the west African country if they wished.

The US has agreed to extend visitor visas for Liberians from 12 to 36 months and pledged $124m in assistance as part of the arrangement.

Under a series of often-secret agreements, the Trump administration has deported thousands of people to nearly two dozen countries that are not their own, advocates say, with about 10 of them in Africa. A new report by Refugees International and Human Rights First say the Trump administration has reached deals with at least 35 countries and has sent roughly 23,000 people to 26 of them as of early August, and makes the Liberia agreement the largest single arrangement so far.

Immigration lawyers have said the Trump administration uses deportations to third countries as a legal loophole to indirectly force asylum seekers back to their home countries.

In many cases, migrants are deported to countries they have never been to or where they face safety risks and are left with little choice other than to return to the home countries they were fleeing from.

A February report by Senate foreign relations committee Democrats found the Trump administration had paid more than $32m to five governments, several with poor human rights records, to accept about 300 third-country deportees – including $1.1m per person to Rwanda for seven deportees, and $7.5m to Equatorial Guinea for 29, a sum exceeding all US aid to that country over the previous eight years.

The report found more than 80% of those sent to third countries had since returned home anyway, often at further cost to taxpayers, and cited cases where deportees with US court-ordered protections were removed to Ghana and Equatorial Guinea before being sent onward within days.

The state department disputed the report’s characterization of its enforcement record.

The Associated Press contributed reporting

world.title: More than 100 dead after goldmine collapses in Central African Republic
world.snippet: The collapse was caused by a landslide, while local officials say the death toll is likely to rise as recovery efforts continue More than...
world.content:
More than 100 people have died after an artisanal goldmine at a small village in western Central African Republic (CAR) caved in due to a landslide, local officials and aid workers said on Wednesday.

The landslide happened on Tuesday afternoon in the village of Zamboye, about 50km (31 miles) from the town of Baboua and close to the border of Cameroon. Footage on social media appeared to show an avalanche of sand descend on a group of people, likely the miners, and cover them.

A statement by a local public prosecutor said many others were trapped under the deluge. It did not mention the number of fatalities. However, Gervais Ganagoroh, a Red Cross volunteer involved in the relief effort, told the Associated Press news agency on Wednesday that more than 100 bodies had been recovered from the collapse and ⁠a senior official at a local mining association confirmed that number to Reuters.

Local media in CAR reported that authorities had launched an investigation into the incident. A second prosecutor from Baboua told the press that the incident is believed to have been caused by “the collapse of several underground tunnels in which miners were operating”.

“The ground completely collapsed and buried people,” Cedric Mbango, a miner at the site, told the AFP news agency, describing the incident as “catastrophic”.

Rescuers are racing to retrieve the bodies of victims and find survivors among the miners, believed to be nationals of CAR and Cameroon. Authorities in Cameroon’s Eastern region said at least three of its citizens have been identified as victims in the incident.

Grégoire Mvongo, the region’s governor told state-owned radio on Wednesday that he was “working in close collaboration with our Central African colleagues to deal with the aftermath of this tragedy”.

Bertrand Be Yangué, a member of the Zamboye youth council, said that “finding them alive would be a miracle.” He added: “We are saddened and heartbroken to see young men and women perish after coming to the mines to save their families from despair.”

The toll is expected to rise as the rescue efforts continue, added Yangué.

The Central African news website Corbeau News reported that heavy machinery, including tractors, was being used in the retrieval mission and could jeopardise the rescue of those still alive under the landmass.

The exact number of people who were in the mine at the time of the cave-in remains unknown.

Small scale artisanal mines are common in different parts of Africa, despite regulations criminalising them, as unemployment continues to drive able-bodied men to abandoned or unused mines, to eke a living. The mining sites often operate with weak safety standards leading to repeated incidents: at least 40 people have died in several mining incidents in CAR this year alone.

world.title: Five Americans among seven killed in safari helicopter crash in Kenya
world.snippet: Officials say all seven people onboard killed, including Telemundo executive and Ecuador intelligence chief Seven people, including five ...
world.content:
Seven people, including five Americans, were killed when a safari helicopter crashed on Wednesday morning in a remote part of northern Kenya, according to local police and the state department.

Among the dead were an executive with Telemundo, the US-based Spanish-language network owned by NBC Universal, and the director of Ecuador’s national intelligence service.

The helicopter crashed at 9.13am while flying from the Loisaba Conservancy to the Ewaso Nyiro area in Samburu county, according to the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority, which said in a statement that an investigation was under way. It said there were seven people onboard – six passengers and the pilot.

Late on Wednesday, David Nkoroi, the police commander for Samburu, told reporters that all seven people onboard had died.

In Washington, the state department said five of those killed were US citizens. “The US embassy is in touch with local authorities and is providing consular assistance,” it said. “We extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones on their loss.”

The identities of the victims were not revealed but a local television station in Miami, Florida, said that José Suárez, 55, president and GM of several Telemundo stations in Florida, was among those killed.

“We are heartbroken to learn the tragic news that José was killed in a helicopter accident in Kenya,” the NBC affiliate in Miami quoted from a joint statement from NBC Universal and Telemundo leadership.

The helicopter crashed in a rugged area in the foothills of Mount Ololokwe, a popular tourist destination in the country, local media reported. The helicopter, owned by local company Lady Lori Helicopters, was carrying guests with the travel company +Beyond.

Lady Lori Helicopters said in a statement that the aircraft was operating a charter flight when it crashed.

Tropic Air Kenya, a local safari operator, said in a statement that it dispatched two of its helicopters to aid search and rescue operations.

The aviation authority said the aircraft was a Eurocopter EC130 B4.

Ecuador confirmed later on Wednesday that Michele Sensi-Contugi, director of the country’s national intelligence center, died in the helicopter crash in Kenya.

In a statement posted on X, the presidency said: “In this moment of deep sorrow, the government extends its heartfelt condolences to his family, loved ones and close associates.”

Sensi-Contugi was visiting Kenya as a tourist with his wife, Stephany Hollihan Vasconez, who also died in the crash. She was a US and Ecuadorian citizen. They are survived by their two children.

Helicopter crashes have happened with increasing regularity in Kenya, which has a thriving tourism industry that depends on domestic carriers to ferry visitors to distant places like Mount Ololokwe.

In February, a legislator was among six people who died after a helicopter crash in a hilly area of western Kenya.

world.title: Spain to allow 500 children in Ceuta to go to mainland in immigration U-turn
world.snippet: Madrid government changes stance after previously saying anyone who entered territory illegally would be sent back Europe live – latest u...
world.content:
The Spanish government has U-turned and said it will allow 500 migrant children in Ceuta to relocate to the mainland.

The majority of the estimated 70,000 people who crossed into Ceuta – a Spanish territory on the coast of north Africa – on 30 July have returned to Morocco. However, under Spanish law, the state has a duty of care to young, unaccompanied migrants until they reach the age of 18.

On 13 August, the interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, had said: “Anyone who illegally enters Ceuta or Melilla [another Spanish enclave in north Africa] knows they will be sent back because Spain and Morocco work together to this end. They will not reach the peninsula, nor the European continent and nor will they remain indefinitely in Ceuta or Melilla.”

The transfer of the children to the Spanish mainland is a sensitive political topic as several regions governed jointly by the conservative People’s party and the far-right Vox are reluctant or opposed to receiving their quota.

To minimise conflict, the youth ministry, in coordination with the Ceuta government, is devising an urgent plan under which NGOs and child protection agencies take charge of the most vulnerable children, girls in particular, without transferring their guardianship to Spain’s regional governments.

Rubén Pérez Correa, the secretary of state for children, has been in Ceuta since Sunday in an effort to resolve a situation in which hundreds of children are living on the street and existing on handouts from Ceuta residents.

News of the government’s plan came only hours after the European Commission said that under EU law all of the migrants should be returned to Morocco. Asked to clarify, the commission’s spokesperson on internal affairs, Markus Lammert, said that by law all irregular migrants remaining in Ceuta should be sent back, “including unaccompanied minors”.

The People’s party has rejected the government plan, saying the best place for the children is with their families. “If Morocco has asked for the children to be returned and if Europe says the illegal immigrants should all be returned, whether children or not, what more does the government need?” the People’s party deputy finance spokesperson, Juan Bravo, said in a television interview.

The mixed messages partly derive from the fact the latest European pact on immigration has not yet been incorporated into Spanish law and therefore Spain’s own legislation on the treatment of unaccompanied minors remains in force.

According to Spain’s ministry of inclusion and migration, as of last March 21,104 people aged 16-23 were under guardianship of the state, of whom about 3,500 were under 17. Approximately 50% were from Morocco. Girls made up about 8% of the total.

world.title: Ebola outbreak in Democratic Republic of the Congo now deadliest in country’s history
world.snippet: At least 2,325 people have died from the virus, according to official data, with outbreak on track to be biggest in history The Ebola out...
world.content:
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is now the deadliest in the country’s history, with at least 2,325 people dead, according to government data, surpassing the toll from the 2018-20 outbreak.

The DRC’s public health institute said confirmed cases had risen to 4,945, including 101 detected in the previous 24 hours.

The World Health Organization has said the outbreak is on track to surpass west Africa’s 2014-16 Ebola outbreak as the biggest in history. The 2014-16 outbreak resulted in 28,616 cases and 11,325 deaths across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, according to WHO data.

On Friday, the UN said Ebola “is winning in the Democratic Republic of the Congo” and said the epidemic was killing one person every 30 minutes.

Six of DRC’s 26 provinces have been affected, mainly those along the country’s north-eastern border. More than 3,400 of the cases have been recorded in Ituri province, where the outbreak was first reported.

The latest numbers of confirmed cases of Ebola in the DRC have made this outbreak – the 17th in the country’s history – the fastest-growing in the known history of the virus. It took almost five months for the 2014-16 west Africa outbreak to reach 1,000 deaths, compared with more than 2,000 deaths in less than three months in this outbreak.

There are no approved vaccines or treatments yet for the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus that is responsible for the current surge in cases. Nonetheless, 1,000 people in the DRC have recovered from the infection, with 730 still in healthcare or isolation facilities.

Clinical trials of two possible treatments for the strain began last month in Ituri. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO director general, said last week that two vaccines developed specifically for Bundibugyo were now being tested on people.

Thomas Parisch, a public health specialist recently deployed to the DRC with Médecins Sans Frontières, said: “Normally, as an outbreak progresses, the case fatality ratio should fall as contact tracing improves and patients are identified and treated earlier. Instead, we’re still seeing many cases detected very late, when treatment is less likely to succeed, with many identified only after they die in the community.”

Uganda has reported at least 20 cases, all in the capital, Kampala. The last case reported there was on 21 June and no community transmission has been recorded. The government declared the country Ebola-free on 28 July after the last Ebola patient, a Congolese national, was discharged on 16 July.

In May, the WHO declared the outbreak in the DRC and Uganda as a public health emergency of international concern. It said sequencing showed the outbreak had started months earlier, in February.

Ebola is transmitted to people from wild animals and then spreads in the human population through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs or other body fluids of infected people, including dead bodies, and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding or clothing.

According to the WHO, symptoms can include fever, fatigue, malaise, muscle pain, headache and sore throat. These are followed by vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, rash and symptoms of impaired kidney and liver functions.

The response to this outbreak has been hampered by attacks on healthcare facilities, often fuelled by misinformation about safe burial practices, as well as strikes by some unpaid health workers. Decades of unrest and outside interference on traumatised communities, as well as poor health and road infrastructure have also complicated the picture.

More than 70% of people die in the community and not in health centres, said Mohamed Janabi, the WHO’s regional Africa director.

Jean-Paul Malo Lotsima, a civil society official in the Djugu area of Ituri, told the AFP news agency: “People prefer to be treated at home, thinking it is a case of poisoning or some other illness.”

He added: “It’s often at the last minute, when the family realises that the situation is getting worse, that patients are taken to hospital. And sometimes, they die on the way.”

Flavier Ngurima, who lives in Nizi, one of the hotspots of the outbreak in Ituri, said his brother died before reaching the treatment centre. “We had called on a nurse from the family to treat him at home because the patient and the family members were afraid to go to the ETC [treatment centre],” he said. “They said that over there, a lot of people die.”
